chicken-breast-baked-broiled-or-roasted-.title: Chicken breast, baked, broiled, or roasted, skin eaten, from raw

content.title: About
content.content: Chicken breast is a lean, boneless cut taken from the bird’s chest. When baked, broiled, or roasted, it retains a high protein content and low fat, especially when the skin is removed. It is a staple in weight‑controlled diets, sports nutrition, and cuisines worldwide.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: A 100 g serving provides about 31 g of high‑quality protein, making it one of the richest protein sources among meats.
If the skin is left on, it adds roughly 15 % fat, but removing it drops total fat to under 3 g per 100 g.
Chicken is the most widely produced poultry globally, accounting for over 50 % of all meat and egg production.
Baking at 180 °C preserves most B‑vitamins, especially niacin (vitamin B3).
Chicken breast appears in dishes from sushi rolls to salads and sandwiches across Asian, European, and American cuisines.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Protein supports muscle growth and repair, immune function, and enzyme synthesis.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Skin‑less breast contains less than 3 g of fat per 100 g, suitable for low‑fat dietary plans.

items.title: Rich in B‑vitamins
items.content: Niacin, vitamin B6, and vitamin B12 aid energy metabolism and nervous system health.

items.title: Source of minerals
items.content: Provides phosphorus, selenium, and zinc, important for bones, antioxidant defense, and immunity.

items.title: Supports weight management
items.content: The satiety effect of protein can help reduce overall calorie intake.

items.title: Food‑borne infection risk
items.content: Undercooked chicken may harbor Salmonella or Campylobacter; cook to an internal temperature of 75 °C.

items.title: Poultry allergy
items.content: A small number of individuals may experience allergic reactions to chicken proteins.

items.title: Added sodium in processed forms
items.content: Pre‑marinated or ready‑to‑eat chicken breasts often contain extra salt, which can be problematic for hypertension.

items.title: Nutrient loss with overcooking
items.content: Excessive heat can degrade B‑vitamins and create harmful compounds such as acrylamide.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Chicken breast can be served hot, sliced thin for salads, formed into patties, baked with herbs and spices, or added to soups. The skin may be kept for extra flavor, but removing it reduces calories.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Fresh raw breast should be kept in the refrigerator at 0‑4 °C for no more than 2 days. Frozen breast retains quality for up to 9 months at –18 °C. Cooked breast stored in an airtight container lasts 3‑4 days in the fridge.

chicken-or-turkey-creole-without-rice.title: Chicken or turkey creole, without rice

content.title: About
content.content: Chicken or turkey creole without rice is a fragrant Creole‑style dish made with tender poultry, tomato sauce, onion, sweet bell pepper, garlic and spices such as paprika, cayenne and oregano. Traditionally served over rice, this version omits the grain, making it lighter and suitable for low‑carb diets.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Creole cuisine originated in Louisiana, blending French, Spanish, African and Native American culinary traditions.
The classic recipe often includes shrimp or sausage, but the poultry‑only version is considered more diet‑friendly.
The dish gained popularity in the United States in the early 20th century through New Orleans restaurants.
Tomatoes and bell pepper give the sauce its bright red color and rich flavor.
Leaving out rice makes the dish appropriate for keto and paleo diets.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Chicken and turkey provide high‑quality protein essential for muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Low in carbohydrates
items.content: Without rice the dish contains fewer carbs, which helps maintain stable blood sugar levels.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Poultry is a good source of B6 and B12 vitamins that support nervous system function and metabolism.

items.title: Antioxidants from tomatoes
items.content: Tomatoes are rich in lycopene, an antioxidant that promotes heart health.

items.title: Lower saturated fat (especially with turkey)
items.content: Turkey contains less saturated fat than beef, making the dish more heart‑friendly.

items.title: Poultry allergy
items.content: Some individuals may be allergic to chicken or turkey, experiencing skin or digestive reactions.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Prepared sauces or broths can be high in sodium; homemade sauce allows better control.

items.title: Undercooked meat
items.content: Insufficiently cooked poultry may harbor harmful bacteria; ensure internal temperature reaches 75 °C.

items.title: Spicy peppers
items.content: Cayenne pepper can irritate the stomach of people with sensitive digestive systems.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the dish hot, garnished with fresh herbs such as parsley or cilantro. Pair it with vegetable sides like broccoli, cauliflower or sautéed zucchini. A squeeze of lime adds extra brightness.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Cool leftovers to room temperature, then store in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3 days. Reheat in the microwave or on a skillet, adding a splash of water to keep the sauce from drying out.

content.title: About
content.content: Creamy Italian dressing is a sauce based on mayonnaise, sour cream and classic Italian herbs such as oregano, basil and garlic. It has a smooth, slightly tangy flavor with aromatic spices, making it perfect for salads, vegetable dishes and marinades.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The dressing combines the traditional taste of Italian vinaigrette with a creamy texture, making it very versatile.
Parmesan cheese is often added, giving it a distinctive cheesy aroma.
It is frequently used as a dip for vegetable sticks and crackers.
It can serve as a light sauce base for pasta dishes.

items.title: Source of vitamin A
items.content: Contains beta‑carotene from carrots and tomatoes, which the body converts to vitamin A to support vision.

items.title: Provides healthy fats
items.content: The mayonnaise base supplies monounsaturated fats that can support heart health when consumed in moderation.

items.title: Rich in antioxidants
items.content: Herbs and spices like oregano and basil contain polyphenols that help combat free radicals.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: Garlic and onion in the recipe stimulate gastric juice production and aid digestion.

items.title: Dairy allergy
items.content: Sour cream and cheese may trigger reactions in people with lactose intolerance or dairy allergy.

items.title: High calorie content
items.content: The creamy base makes the dressing calorie‑dense, so portion control is recommended.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Added salt can be a concern for those monitoring sodium intake.

content.title: How to Use
content.content: Use the dressing to coat green or vegetable salads, as a dip for bread, crackers and veggie sticks, or as a marinade for chicken, fish or vegetables before baking.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in the refrigerator at 0 °C–4 °C in a sealed container. Once opened, it is usually good for 7–10 days. Discard if it develops an off‑odor or changes color.

pork-bacon-smoked-or-cured-cooked.title: Pork Bacon, Smoked or Cured, Cooked

content.title: About
content.content: Pork bacon is a pre‑processed pork product that is smoked or cured and then cooked. It is made from the pork belly, which is salted, sometimes sweetened and spiced, and then smoked over wood. The finished product has a distinctive aroma, firm texture, and rich flavor.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Bacon was known in ancient Rome, where it was called "petaso".
Smoking not only adds flavor but also extends the product’s shelf life.
In the United States bacon is often served as crisp strips, while in Europe it is commonly used in chunks for dishes.
There are several types: smoked, cured, and pre‑cooked (ready to eat).
A traditional English breakfast typically includes bacon, eggs, beans, and tomatoes.

items.title: Protein source
items.content: Bacon provides high‑quality animal protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: It contains thiamine, niacin, and vitamin B12, which support energy metabolism.

items.title: Iron and zinc
items.content: These minerals are important for immune function and blood formation.

items.title: Choline
items.content: Choline supports liver health and nervous system function.

items.title: Satiety
items.content: Rich in protein and fat, bacon can help maintain a feeling of fullness.

items.title: High sodium
items.content: The curing salt makes bacon high in sodium, which can raise blood pressure.

items.title: Saturated fats
items.content: Bacon contains a large proportion of saturated fat, which may affect cholesterol levels when consumed in excess.

items.title: Nitrites and nitrates
items.content: These are often added for preservation and color; high intake may lead to formation of potentially harmful compounds.

items.title: Pork allergy
items.content: A small number of people may have allergic reactions to pork proteins.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Bacon is calorie‑dense, so portion control is advisable, especially on weight‑management diets.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Bacon can be pan‑fried until crisp, baked in the oven, or added to soups, salads, pasta, and omelets. It is also used as a flavor base for sauces and stews.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep bacon in its original packaging or an airtight container in the refrigerator at 0‑4 °C for up to 7‑10 days. For longer storage, freeze it in a vacuum‑sealed bag for up to 3 months. Before use, check for off‑odors or discoloration, which indicate spoilage.
